DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

The pilot is a good basis, and most of the cost arithmetic is correct. But the study misreads its own pilot data in ways that matter. The headline conclusions, a uniform service for houses and flats and full funding, don't survive correction. Fixed, the figures show a likely funding shortfall and a need for a separate approach for flats.

## Major issues

### 1. Participation was not "broadly similar" across housing types

Table 1 shows **66% participation in houses and 21% in flats**. Flats participate at less than a third of the rate of houses. That gap is the most important finding in the pilot, and the text says the opposite. The recommendation for a uniform service rests on this misreading.

Low participation in flats is a well-known national pattern. It is usually caused by lack of storage, communal bin areas and the distance to the collection point. With about 10,400 flats in the district (20% of 52,000), Thornbury needs a flats-specific approach, such as communal food bins, different caddy arrangements or targeted engagement. That approach will carry its own costs.

### 2. The projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear in the pilot

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." Table 1 gives **57%** overall. 64% appears nowhere. The pilot's mix of 80% houses and 20% flats also matches the district's, so 57% is the representative figure.

Recalculated:

| Basis | Annual tonnage |
|---|---|
| Study (64% × 52,000 × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks) | 3,290 t |
| Pilot overall rate (57%) | ~2,930 t |
| By housing type (houses 66% at 1.9 kg; flats 21% at 1.4 kg) | **~2,870 t** |

The by-type calculation is the most defensible. It is about **13% below** the study's figure.

### 3. Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes; the projection needs 2,900–3,300

Section 4 states that Brookfield's contracted capacity is **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Yet the disposal saving assumes all 3,290 tonnes go there at £38 per tonne. Even on corrected tonnage, roughly **1,100 tonnes a year** has no local outlet. That leaves two options:

- **Send it to the plant 46 miles away.** This brings an unknown gate fee plus haulage, and longer trips would probably need extra vehicle and crew time.
- **Leave it in the residual stream.** This gives no saving, and since the Council is legally required to collect food waste separately, it isn't really an option.

The claim that "treatment is local" is true for only about 60% of the tonnage, and only until 2029.

### 4. Once corrected, the service is not fully funded

The cost total checks out: £141,400 + £408,000 + £96,000 + £88,000 = £733,400. The saving per tonne (£112 − £38 = £74) is also right. The problem is the tonnage the saving is applied to:

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | Against £520k allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Study as written | £243,000 | £490,400 | £29,600 surplus |
| Corrected tonnage, ignoring the capacity limit | ~£212,000 | ~£521,000 | **Roughly break-even** |
| Saving limited to Brookfield's 1,800 t | £133,200 | **£600,200** | **~£80,000 shortfall** |

The last row is the realistic one under the current contract. Any costs of sending the excess to the 46-mile plant would come on top. On the paper's own numbers, the service is not fully funded.

Two further funding points:

- The allocation is **provisional**. The paper should say what happens if it's confirmed lower.
- The six vehicles cost about **£990,000 up front**. Depreciation spreads that cost for accounting purposes, but the paper doesn't say how the capital will be found. It also leaves out financing costs.

### 5. Several cost lines are missing

The author says every cost line is shown. Items not visible include:

- **Cover for crew absence.** Six crews of two leave no allowance for leave, sickness or training.
- **Supervision, management and the customer phone line.** Section 6 describes the phone line, but it isn't costed.
- **A spare vehicle**, for breakdowns and servicing.
- **The flats-specific provision** described in issue 1.
- **Haulage and gate fees** for tonnage beyond Brookfield's capacity.
- **One-off launch costs.** It's unclear whether the March 2027 delivery to 52,000 households and recruitment are included in the £88,000 annualised figure.

It's also unclear whether £34,000 per operative includes employer on-costs (national insurance and pension).

## Moderate issues

6. **The pilot probably overstates long-term participation.** Six months captures the novelty effect, and participation often falls after the launch period. "Average weekly set-out" is also not the same as participation, since some households put caddies out every other week. The projection should include a lower-participation scenario.
7. **The satisfaction figure is weaker than it looks.** The 81% is "of surveyed pilot households." Participating households are more likely to respond to a survey, so the figure overstates satisfaction among all residents. The response rate isn't given.
8. **The timetable has no contingency.** It runs as follows:
   - December 2026: vehicle order.
   - March 2027: vehicle delivery, plus caddies delivered to 52,000 households.
   - February–March 2027: recruitment and training.
   - 5 April 2027: launch.

   Food waste vehicles have been in high demand nationally, so a three-month lead time is optimistic. The paper should name a fallback, such as hired vehicles.
9. **Statutory deadline.** Most English councils were required to start weekly food waste collections by 31 March 2026, unless they had a transitional arrangement. The study doesn't mention the deadline. If Thornbury is already past it, Cabinet should know whether the April 2027 start is agreed with Defra. This also strengthens the case for urgency.
10. **Round capacity isn't evidenced.** Six vehicles for 52,000 households is about 1,700 households per vehicle per day, over five days. That may be feasible, but no route modelling is presented, so the vehicle and crew numbers are effectively assumed.

## Minor issues

11. **Table 1's "All" row.** Food waste per participating household is shown as 1.9 kg. The weighted average is 1.86 kg. This is a rounding issue, but it combines with the participation error to inflate the projection.
12. **Two months fewer than the next reprint.** The plan gives each household a three-month supply of liners at launch. Ongoing liner supply should be confirmed within the £88,000 figure.

## The author's description against the document

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| "Participation held up across houses and flats" | **Incorrect.** 66% against 21%. |
| Projections "based on how Thornbury residents actually behave" | The projection uses 64%, which isn't the pilot's figure (57%). |
| "Every cost line is shown" | Several are missing: absence cover, supervision, the phone line, a spare vehicle, provision for flats, and excess haulage. |
| Saving uses Brookfield's gate fee | It applies the fee to about 1,500 tonnes beyond Brookfield's confirmed capacity. |
| Net cost of about £490,000 "fully covered" | The realistic net cost is around £600,000, against a provisional £520,000. |
| "Treatment is local" | True for about 60% of the tonnage, and only until 2029. |
| The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time | Reasonable, but it has no contingency, and the statutory deadline isn't addressed. |

## Suggested revisions

1. Correct the participation text and add a separate delivery model for flats, with its costs.
2. Recalculate tonnage by housing type, and add a lower-participation scenario.
3. Address the 1,800-tonne cap. Cost the second plant, or negotiate more capacity at Brookfield, and show the saving on the tonnage Brookfield can actually take.
4. Restate the net cost against the provisional allocation. Show the shortfall and how it would be met, and explain the capital funding for the vehicles.
5. Complete the cost table and confirm whether the crew costs include on-costs.
6. Add a contingency for vehicle delays, and state the position on the statutory deadline.

The service itself is required and clearly workable. But Cabinet should approve it knowing the realistic net cost and the need for a separate approach to flats, not on the basis that it is uniform and fully funded.
